review: All four final cards fully read. Actual three hiddenness reasons preserved, compatibility distinguished from likelihood, conditional suffering argument distinguished from moral realism, first-person nonbelief and auxiliary cancellation claims calibrated without universal disproof.

cards.words: Horn proposes free choice, believers sharing testimony, and nonautomatic damnation as possible divine reasons for permitting nonbelief, arguing that Lataster has not established strict incompatibility.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Horn offers three distinct and understandable reasons why God might permit nonbelief—free choice, believers sharing testimony, and salvation without explicit belief—thereby answering a strict claim of logical incompatibility. Principal limitation: Lataster presented hiddenness probabilistically, so demonstrating possible divine reasons does not show that nonresistant nonbelief is sufficiently expected under classical theism or that these explanations improve its comparative likelihood. Live burden: Horn must support the actual plausibility and predictive relevance of his proposed reasons rather than shifting the burden to Lataster to prove that God could have none. Locked score: 76 The response is concrete, relevant, and partly protective of the God concept, but it answers a stronger contradiction claim than Lataster made and therefore only partially addresses the live evidential challenge.

cards.words: Lataster explains that suffering can be compared with expectations conditional upon God’s existence without assuming objective morality as an independent premise or asserting that evil objectively exists.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Lataster precisely distinguishes conditional expectation from assuming moral realism, showing that the question is what suffering should be expected if God exists rather than whether objective evil is independently established. Principal limitation: This logical clarification supplies no additional reason to classify observed suffering as gratuitous or to conclude that its likelihood is lower under classical theism than under relevant alternatives. Live burden: He must still defend the substantive likelihood comparison after correctly showing that moral realism is unnecessary for formulating the probabilistic argument from suffering. Locked score: 86 The short reply is exceptionally coherent, responsive, precise, and calibrated because it removes Horn’s claimed presupposition at the decisive point, while appropriately leaving the original evidential comparison to stand or fall upon its separate support.

cards.words: Lataster uses his willing nonbelief to argue that a loving, knowing, powerful God desiring his salvation and relationship would be expected to provide personally convincing evidence.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Lataster’s first-person case concretely connects divine goodness, knowledge, and power to an expected successful revelation, while his stated willingness to believe and follow distinguishes nonresistance from hostile rejection. Principal limitation: One sincere self-report cannot establish the prevalence or full comparative likelihood of nonresistant nonbelief, and the assumed relationship between salvation, revelation, and the specified deity still requires examination. Live burden: He must show why his case is substantially less expected under classical theism and how strongly it favors no God or differently motivated gods over Horn’s proposed explanation. Locked score: 84 The argument is coherent, clear, well calibrated, and centrally relevant because it connects each attribute to a concrete observation without claiming disproof, but limited generalizability and undeveloped likelihood magnitudes constrain its evidential force.

cards.words: Lataster argues that auxiliary explanations carry prior costs and that unmistakable knowledge of God’s existence would still permit a person freely to reject, disobey, or refuse worship.
cards.critique: Strongest feature: Lataster directly answers Horn’s freedom concern by distinguishing awareness of God’s existence from choosing obedience, supported by examples of informed rejection rather than epistemic ignorance or compelled worship. Principal limitation: He does not establish that the prior cost of every auxiliary explanation exactly cancels its improvement in conditional likelihood, and dismissing all proposed reasons as excuses understates their possible relevance. Live burden: He must compare the actual probabilistic effects of Horn’s reasons while preserving the valid point that unmistakable awareness and voluntary rejection can coexist. Locked score: 83 The reply is highly responsive, conceptually clear, and important to the hiddenness dispute, but its unsupported no-change calculation and rhetorical characterization keep the probabilistic conclusion less secure than the freedom rebuttal.
